806.title: Plant for later
806.hook: Honi's carob tree again: what will grow after you? (Talmud, Taanit 23a)
806.howItsDone: Some people answer a death by planting: a memorial tree, a scholarship, a garden bed, or simply passing on a recipe or skill the person taught them, so that something keeps growing after the loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life pressed into a line on a stone. Your line was six words. Did yours come, and did you write it down? Day eight hundred six.

A man is walking along a road and sees someone on his knees in the dirt, planting a carob tree. The walker stops and asks how long it will take before the tree bears fruit. Seventy years, says the planter. The walker asks the obvious next question: are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? The walker is Honi, a sage the Talmud remembers in the tractate Taanit, and this may not be the first time you've met him on this path. Today the story comes back, at the end of a block about grief, with a new question: what will grow after you?
screen: `A MAN PLANTING A CAROB TREE.` → `"SEVENTY YEARS."` → `WHAT GROWS AFTER YOU?`

segments.voice: First, the planter's answer. In the Talmud's telling, he says, more or less: I found the world with carob trees in it. As my ancestors planted for me, so I plant for my children. He isn't planting for himself. He's paying forward a gift he never saw being given. Second, Honi sleeps. Honi sits down to eat, sleep comes over him, and a rock formation closes around him so that no one sees him. He sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree, and asks: are you the one who planted it? The man answers: I'm his grandson. Third, an ending that isn't sweet. The Talmud doesn't stop there. Honi goes home and to the house of study, and nobody believes he is who he says. No one gives him the honor he was used to. In his loneliness he asks for death, and he dies. Some readers hear the two halves of the story together: a tree can outlive its planter, and a person still needs companions while they're alive. Fourth, what the dead leave planted. In a week of grief, the story turns the question around. The people we've lost planted things we still eat from: a recipe, a way of giving thanks at the table, a habit of showing up, a garden, a joke the family still tells. And the living can plant too, things whose fruit they won't be around to taste. The instruction is short: plant for later.
screen: `AS MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME` · `HONI SLEEPS, THE TREE GROWS` · `AN ENDING THAT ISN'T SWEET` · `WHAT THE DEAD LEFT PLANTED` · then, large: `PLANT FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing someone before you planted that you still live from: a recipe, a saying, a habit, a skill they taught you, an actual tree. Give them a moment of thanks, in whatever way is yours. Then choose one small thing you could begin that will outlast this week, maybe this life: a seed in a pot, a letter to a child to open later, teaching someone a skill, a kindness made into a habit. Hold that one thing in mind. The bell holds the time.
Plant for later: doing something now whose fruit you may never taste, as others once did for you. Today's word.
Your line: plant for later. Today, begin the one thing you chose, even if the first step is small enough to fit in a pocket. Day eight hundred six.

807.title: Calm at the end
807.hook: your own last day, seen calmly and kindly
807.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius reflect briefly on the day as if it were their last, often in the evening, aiming to be steady rather than frightened; others do a gentle version as a short sit, and stop whenever it feels too heavy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Honi and the carob tree. Your line was plant for later. Did you start one thing that will grow after this week is gone? Today, a quiet look toward the end of a life: your own. Day eight hundred seven.

An exercise that sounds grim on paper turns out, for some people, to be strangely gentle. No hospital alarms, no movie music, no deathbed speech. Just an ordinary last day, seen from a distance, the way you'd look at a field from the top of a hill. A Roman emperor wrote reminders to himself about this in a book we now call the Meditations. He wasn't trying to frighten himself. He was trying to steady himself. Today we borrow his steadiness and add one softer word to it: kindly.
screen: `NO ALARMS, NO MUSIC.` → `A FIELD SEEN FROM A HILL.` → `CALMLY, AND KINDLY.`

segments.voice: First, who he's talking to. In the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius keeps saying thou, and the thou is Marcus. He isn't lecturing a crowd. He's talking himself down. Second, every day as the last. In George Long's translation, he writes: "The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite." Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say cram every day full. He doesn't say panic. Third, the road between two ditches. Violently excited is one ditch: the frantic version, a rush to do everything at once. Torpid is the other: numb, flat, looking away. Marcus walks the road between them, and that road is the calm. Seen this way, the thought of a last day isn't a fire alarm. It works more like a carpenter's level, a quiet tool that shows what is straight and what has drifted. Fourth, kindly. Marcus could be hard on himself. Today adds something gentler: look at that last day the way you'd look at a friend's. If what comes up is tenderness for your own small, ordinary life, that isn't a failure of calm. It may be part of it. And if you're grieving, or ill, or the thought is simply too heavy today, setting it down is a calm choice too.
screen: `HE'S TALKING TO HIMSELF.` · `EVERY DAY AS THE LAST.` · `NEITHER FRANTIC NOR NUMB.` · `KINDLY, TOO.` · then, large: `CALM AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, gently. Sit comfortably and let your breathing settle on its own. Now let an ordinary last day come to mind, without illness and without detail: a window, some light, a voice you love somewhere nearby. You don't need to see it clearly. Try the road between the ditches: not rushing toward the picture, not turning away from it. Then let one kind thought toward your own life arrive, or don't, and just rest. If at any point it feels too heavy, open your eyes and come back to the room. That counts as doing it. The bell holds the time.
Calm at the end. Facing your own last day neither frantic nor numb, and with kindness, as Marcus tried to in his Meditations. Today's word.
Your line: calm at the end. Today, when something small rattles you, look at it once from that calm window, and let it be the size it really is. Day eight hundred seven.

808.title: From the end
808.hook: decide one thing by what you'd value on your last day
808.howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats and spiritual direction, a person facing a decision may be guided to consider, in prayer, what they would wish they had chosen at the point of death; others use the same question informally when making choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus and the road between two ditches. Your line was calm at the end. Did anything small look smaller from that calm window? Today, we stand at that window on purpose, to choose. Day eight hundred eight.

Two options on the kitchen table. Maybe two jobs, or two weekends, or one hard phone call you keep moving to next week. You've made the list of pros and cons, and the columns come out even. You've asked three friends and gotten three answers. Some decisions just sit there, refusing to tip. Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuits, wrote a small book of prayer exercises, and tucked inside it is a strange tool for exactly this moment. It asks you to stand somewhere else before you choose.
screen: `TWO OPTIONS, EVEN COLUMNS.` → `THREE FRIENDS, THREE ANSWERS.` → `A TOOL FROM IGNATIUS.`

segments.voice: First, a book for choosing. The Spiritual Exercises are a set of prayers and meditations, and part of the book is about making a choice, which Ignatius calls an election. He doesn't offer one method. He offers several, for different kinds of moments, including the moments when nothing seems clear. Second, stand at the end. One of his ways, in plain paraphrase, goes like this: consider, as if you were at the point of death, what way of deciding this present matter you would then wish you had chosen. And then choose that way now. It's a change of seat. Instead of asking what you want this week, you ask what you'd be glad of from the last chair. Third, a neighbor's tool. In the same few lines Ignatius offers a cousin of it: picture a person you've never met who brings you this exact choice, and notice what you'd advise them. Then take your own advice. Both tools do the same thing. They step you out of the knot, so the choice can be seen whole. Fourth, the setting. For Ignatius, this happens inside prayer, as a way of seeking what God wants, and Jesuits and others who give the Exercises still teach it that way. People outside that faith sometimes borrow the shape of it as a quiet thinking tool. Either way, the question is the same, and it's surprisingly practical: from the end, which of these will I be glad I chose?
screen: `A BOOK FOR CHOOSING.` · `STAND AT THE END.` · `ADVISE A STRANGER.` · `INSIDE PRAYER, AND OUTSIDE IT.` · then, large: `FROM THE END.`

segments.voice: Bring one small choice to mind, something real but not enormous: how to spend this evening, whether to send a message, what to say yes to. Hold both options lightly. Now sit for a moment in that last chair, calm, with the day almost done. From there, look back at this choice. Which way would you be glad of? Don't argue with the answer, and don't force one if it doesn't come. If you pray, you can bring the choice into prayer the way Ignatius did. Then make the choice, or simply rest. The bell holds the time.
From the end. Making a present choice by asking what you would wish you had chosen, seen from your last day. A tool from Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises. Today's word.
Your line: from the end. Today, make one choice from that last chair, even a small one, and notice whether it feels different from choosing by the to-do list. Day eight hundred eight.

809.title: An object to remember
809.hook: Stoics, monks and painters kept a skull or a small object as a reminder
809.howItsDone: Some people keep a small object on a desk or in a pocket as a memento mori, a reminder of death that keeps the day in proportion; in some traditions it has been a skull, a cross or prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius and the last chair. Your line was from the end. Did you make one choice from there? Today, a way to keep that chair close, sitting on a shelf. Day eight hundred nine.

A desk in an old Dutch painting. A book left open. A candle burned down to a stub. An hourglass with most of the sand at the bottom. A pocket watch. And, sitting calmly among them, a human skull. Painters made whole still lifes like this, and art historians call them vanitas paintings, from the Latin for vanity, the word that echoes through Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, all is vanity. They weren't horror pictures. They were reminders, made to hang in a room where someone would see them every day. Today: the small object that does the remembering for you.
screen: `A CANDLE, AN HOURGLASS, A SKULL.` → `A PAINTING THAT REMINDS.` → `AN OBJECT THAT REMEMBERS FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the skull on the desk. In those paintings the objects talk to each other. The candle is burning, the sand is falling, the flowers are about to drop their petals. The skull just says it plainly. The Latin phrase people attach to these pictures is memento mori: remember that you will die. Second, death before your eyes. In the Handbook of the Stoic teacher Epictetus, the advice, in paraphrase, is to keep death and every other thing that seems terrible before your eyes daily, and death most of all. Then, he says, you'll never think a mean thought or crave anything beyond measure. For him, the reminder wasn't gloom. It was a way of keeping desire the right size. Third, a skull in a play. In Shakespeare, the gravedigger hands Hamlet a skull, and Hamlet learns whose it was: the jester he loved as a boy. "Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio." The scene turns a bone into a person, and a person into a question. Tradition says some monks kept a skull in their cells for the same reason; others kept a cross, or a few beads. Fourth, any small object will do. None of these things is magic. A skull, a coin, a smooth stone, a dried leaf: each works like a knot tied in a handkerchief. You set it where your eye lands, and it quietly asks the question for you, on the days you'd forget to ask it yourself.
screen: `THE SKULL ON THE DESK.` · `DEATH BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `ALAS, POOR YORICK.` · `ANY SMALL OBJECT WILL DO.` · then, large: `AN OBJECT TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Look around you, or think of what's in your pocket or on your desk. Choose one small object: a stone, a key, a coin, a leaf, a photograph. It doesn't need to be grim. Hold it, or rest your eyes on it. Let it mean one simple thing: this day is not forever, so let it count. Breathe with it for a while. Then decide where it will live, somewhere you'll see it tomorrow morning without trying. The bell holds the time.
An object to remember. A small thing you keep in sight, like a painter's skull or Epictetus's daily reminder, so it can ask the question for you. Today's word.
Your line: an object to remember. Today, each time your eye lands on the object you chose, take one breath and let it remind you that this day counts. Day eight hundred nine.

810.title: A letter for after
810.hook: a letter to be read after you're gone
810.howItsDone: In Jewish tradition, an ethical will, a tsavaah, is a letter of values, blessings and requests left for family; some people of other paths also write letters to be read after their death, sometimes kept with a legal will.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a skull on a painter's desk and Hamlet in the graveyard. Your line was an object to remember. Did your object catch your eye today? Today, something you leave behind on purpose: words. Day eight hundred ten.

An envelope in a drawer, with one line on the front: to be opened after I'm gone. Inside there's no list of bank accounts and nothing about who gets the good chairs. Just a page about what the writer learned, what they hope for, what they'd like forgiven. In Jewish tradition this kind of letter has a name, an ethical will, and some families still write and keep them. The idea is far older than envelopes. Today: the letter for after, and a few people in old books who wrote one out loud.
screen: `TO BE OPENED AFTER I'M GONE.` → `NO MONEY, NO CHAIRS.` → `AN ETHICAL WILL.`

segments.voice: First, Jacob gathers his sons. In Genesis, the old man calls his family to his bed: "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days." What follows is a long speech to each son by name. Some of it is blessing and some of it is blunt. It isn't a will about property. It's a father saying who he thinks each of them is. Second, a farewell. In the second letter to Timothy, the writer sounds like someone near the end: "the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Some readers hear the whole letter as a farewell, written for after. Third, a will made of words. The Hebrew word for a will is tsavaah, and the ethical will borrows it for something different: not who gets what, but what mattered. Some are a few sentences long. Some are pages of advice, apology and thanks. Rabbis wrote them, and so did ordinary parents. Fourth, first lines only. Nobody needs to write the whole letter today. A first line is enough to find out what you'd want to say. And once a line is written for after, it has a way of asking whether it could be said now.
screen: `JACOB GATHERS HIS SONS.` · `A FAREWELL TO TIMOTHY.` · `A WILL MADE OF WORDS.` · `FIRST LINES ONLY.` · then, large: `A LETTER FOR AFTER.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and paper, or a note on your phone. Think of one person who might one day read a letter from you. Don't plan the whole thing. Let the first lines come: maybe what you hope for them, or one thing you learned, or one thing you're grateful for. Write two or three sentences, no more. If nothing comes, write their name and sit with it. Then put it somewhere safe, or simply let it go. The bell holds the time.
A letter for after. Words written to be read once you're gone, like Jacob's blessings or a Jewish ethical will: not property, but what mattered. Today's word.
Your line: after me. Today, read your first lines once more, and ask whether any of them could be said to that person sooner. Day eight hundred ten.

811.title: Nothing unsaid
811.hook: make peace before you have to
811.howItsDone: Some Christians take Matthew 5:23–24 as a reason to seek reconciliation before worship or communion, and some Jews ask people's forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacob's sons around his bed and the ethical will. Your line was after me. Did any of your first lines want to be said sooner? Today, the hardest kind of thing to leave unsaid. Day eight hundred eleven.

An offering in his hands, a man stands in the temple courtyard. It's a holy moment, the kind he's been preparing for. And right then, of all times, a face comes to mind: a brother he quarreled with, who still has something against him. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells him exactly what to do with that offering. His answer puts the altar second. Today: making peace before you have to, and why one teacher would let a holy moment wait for it.
screen: `AN OFFERING IN HIS HANDS.` → `A BROTHER COMES TO MIND.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: First, leave the gift at the altar. In Matthew, Jesus says: "if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Notice the order. The worship waits. The mending goes first. Second, before the Day of Atonement. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, says something close to this about Yom Kippur. In paraphrase: the day atones for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between a person and a neighbor, it does not atone until the person makes peace with that neighbor. In the days before Yom Kippur, some Jews call or visit people to ask forgiveness. Third, before the sun goes down. In the letter to the Ephesians, the advice gets a clock: "let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Anger isn't forbidden in the verse. Carrying it overnight is what it warns against. Fourth, one small mend. None of these texts asks for a grand scene. A message, a short apology, an honest sentence is often enough to start. And making peace never means putting yourself back in harm's way. If someone isn't safe for you, peace can be something you make inside yourself, or with help, without contacting them at all. The point of the week's theme is simple: there's no need to wait for a deathbed to do this.
screen: `LEAVE THE GIFT AT THE ALTAR.` · `BEFORE THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · `BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN.` · `ONE SMALL MEND.` · then, large: `NOTHING UNSAID.`

segments.voice: Let one small, unfinished thing come to mind: a sharp word you said, a message you never answered, a coolness with someone that never got explained. Choose something small and safe, not the biggest wound in your life. Breathe with it for a moment. Then let the first sentence of a mend form in your head, plain and short. You don't have to send it yet. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer for a breath or two. Then rest, and let it be. The bell holds the time.
Nothing unsaid. Making peace while there's still time, the way Jesus sends the man away from the altar and the Mishnah asks for peace before Yom Kippur. Today's word.
Your line: nothing unsaid. Before the sun goes down today, send or say that first small sentence, if it's safe and it's yours to say. Day eight hundred eleven.

812.title: Say it now
812.hook: tell someone what they mean to you
812.howItsDone: Some families and friends make a habit of telling each other what they mean while they are alive, through letters, toasts at gatherings or a simple message, rather than saving it for a eulogy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gift left at the altar. Your line was nothing unsaid. Did a first small sentence of peace get sent? Today, the week's last day, and the other kind of unsaid thing: the good kind. Day eight hundred twelve.

At a funeral, someone stands up and says beautiful things. How kind she was. How he always showed up. How the whole family leaned on her without ever saying so. Everyone nods, and some people cry, and the one person who would most have loved to hear it is the one person who can't. A eulogy is a gift with no address. Today: three people in old books who said what someone meant to them, and the difference it makes to say it while the other person is still in the room.
screen: `BEAUTIFUL WORDS AT A FUNERAL.` → `A GIFT WITH NO ADDRESS.` → `SAID WHILE THEY'RE IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: First, David's lament. When Jonathan dies in battle, David sings a lament for him, and one tender line comes after the news: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me." It's a beautiful line. Jonathan never hears it in the song. Second, Ruth on the road. Ruth's husband has died, and her mother-in-law Naomi tells her to go home to her own people. Ruth answers while Naomi can still hear: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Those words are said to a living face, on a dusty road, and they change what happens next. Third, Paul names his friends. Near the end of his letter to the Romans, Paul stops teaching and starts greeting people by name. "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus." Name after name, with a few words about each. A long list that amounts to saying: you mattered to me. Fourth, one sentence, today. It doesn't need to be a speech. One plain sentence will do: you made this year easier; I think of you when I hear that song; I'm glad you're in my life. And a look back at the week: plant for later, calm at the end, from the end, an object to remember, after me, nothing unsaid, and now say it now. Each one turned the end of life back toward today.
screen: `DAVID'S LAMENT FOR JONATHAN.` · `RUTH SAYS IT ON THE ROAD.` · `PAUL NAMES HIS FRIENDS.` · `ONE SENTENCE, TODAY.` · then, large: `SAY IT NOW.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who means something to you and may not know it, or may not have heard it lately. A friend, a parent, a teacher, a neighbor, a child. Hold their face for a few breaths. Now find one plain sentence that says what they mean to you. Not a speech, just true. Say it quietly in your head until it sounds like you.
